extracted.intended_audience: design owners, applicants and their representatives seeking international registration of industrial designs under the Hague Agreement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and filing an international application to register industrial designs under the Hague Agreement (WIPO), including eligibility, required contents, fees, examination procedures, duration, renewals and post-registration changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to file (Who May Use the Hague System)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be entitled to file an international application an applicant must satisfy at least one condition: (a) be a national of a Contracting Party (or member State of an intergovernmental organization party to the Agreement), (b) have a domicile in the territory of a Contracting Party, or (c) have a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in the territory of a Contracting Party. Under the 1999 Act, habitual residence in a Contracting Party is an additional basis for filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Contracting Party through which entitlement is claimed is the 'State of origin' (1960 Act) or the 'applicant's Contracting Party' (1999 Act). A person lacking these entitlements must file nationally or regionally. Be careful to establish entitlement before filing internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where protection may be requested (Act compatibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection can only be obtained in Contracting Parties that are party to the same Act (1934/1960/1999) as the Contracting Party through which the applicant claims entitlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If entitlement is claimed through a Party bound only by the 1999 Act, the applicant may request protection only in Parties bound by the 1999 Act; similarly for the 1960 Act. The Hague system cannot protect designs in non‑Contracting Parties; national filing is required for those countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: International application may be first filing (No prior national application required)
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application does not require any prior national application or registration; a design can be protected for the first time at the international level through the Hague Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may file internationally as their first filing—no national priority is necessary (though priority claims are possible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and form of the international application
rubrics_metrics.description: The international application must be filed in English, French or Spanish (at the applicant’s option) on the official form provided by the International Bureau of WIPO; electronic filing (E‑filing) is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the official WIPO form (available on WIPO website) and consider e‑filing for convenience. Choose one of the three permitted languages at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents: reproductions and designations
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must contain a reproduction of the industrial designs concerned, together with the designation of the Contracting Parties where protection is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reproductions meet quality standards (see formal examination). Clearly list all desired designations; only designated Parties will be examined and potentially grant protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple designs per application: limit and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application may include up to 100 different designs, provided all designs belong to the same class of the Locarno (International) Classification of Industrial Designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group designs by Locarno class; exceeding 100 designs or mixing classes will not comply. Plan filings to respect classification limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferred publication periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant may request deferred publication: up to 12 months from filing (1960 Act) or up to 30 months from filing (1999 Act), or from the priority date where priority is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deferment if you wish to delay public disclosure; choose the applicable maximum depending on which Act applies to your filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees: types and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application is subject to three types of fees (in Swiss francs): a basic fee, a publication fee, and for each designated Contracting Party either a standard fee or an individual fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee schedules and an automatic fee calculator are available on WIPO's website. Applicants from LDCs (or certain intergovernmental organizations) may be eligible for reduced fees (10% of prescribed amount) under specified conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee reductions for certain applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: For applicants whose sole entitlement is a connection with a Least Developed Country (LDC) or with an intergovernmental organization the majority of whose member States are LDCs, filing fees and standard designation fees are reduced to 10% of the prescribed amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the UN list of LDCs and WIPO rules to confirm eligibility before filing to benefit from reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing channel / transmission to the International Bureau
rubrics_metrics.description: The international application is normally sent directly to the International Bureau of WIPO by the applicant or representative. Under the 1960 Act a Contracting Party may require that applications be filed through its own Office when it is considered the State of origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm whether your State of origin imposes a national transmission requirement under the 1960 Act. Otherwise, direct filing to WIPO is standard practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal examination by the International Bureau (formal requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt the International Bureau checks compliance with prescribed formal requirements (e.g., quality of reproductions, payment of required fees). Applicants are informed of defects which must be corrected within three months; failure results in abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure high quality reproductions and timely fee payment. Respond promptly to any defect notices within the three‑month limit to avoid abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Bureau does not conduct substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The International Bureau of WIPO does not appraise novelty or any other substantive ground and is not entitled to reject an international application on substantive grounds; substantive examination is the competence of each designated Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on WIPO to assess novelty; expect each designated Contracting Party to exercise its domestic substantive law (e.g., novelty, originality) during national examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive examination by designated Offices and right to refuse
rubrics_metrics.description: After publication each designated Office must identify registrations in which it is designated and proceed with substantive examination under its domestic legislation. Each Office may refuse protection if the design fails to meet substantive domestic conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A refusal cannot be based on formal requirements (since WIPO has already checked them). Be prepared for differing substantive outcomes across designated Parties and for national procedures/appeals in the event of refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal notification periods (6 months; 12 months option under 1999 Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any refusal must be notified to the International Bureau within six months from publication. Under the 1999 Act, Offices that are Examining Offices or allow opposition may declare the refusal period replaced by 12 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor the Bulletin and be aware of applicable refusal periods for each designated Office; check whether a 12‑month period applies. Time limits govern the opportunity to receive a refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and appeals for refusals at national level
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of refusal the applicant has the same remedies as if filing directly with the Office in question; appeals and remedies are handled solely at the national level within local time limits and procedures. The International Bureau is not involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If refused, pursue appeals or other remedies before the competent national authorities in the designated Contracting Party, following that country's law and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of refusal or issuance of grant statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A refusal may be withdrawn totally or partially, or replaced by a statement that protection is granted for some or all designs. Conversely, where no grounds for refusal are found an Office may issue a statement of grant of protection before the expiry of the refusal period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep track of notifications; withdrawals or grant statements will change the status of protection in the designated Party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of the international registration (legal effect is domestic law)
rubrics_metrics.description: If no refusal is notified (or it is withdrawn), the international registration has the effect as a grant of protection in that Contracting Party under that Party's law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine scope, enforcement, competent authorities and sanctions for infringement, consult the domestic law of each Contracting Party where protection is in force; the Hague system is procedural only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and renewal of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: International registrations are effected for an initial period of five years and may be renewed for additional five‑year periods in respect of each designated Contracting Party, up to the total term allowed by those Parties' laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewals are managed through the International Bureau and must respect each designated Party's maximum term. Track national maximums when planning renewals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal procedure and electronic renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for renewals must be presented to the International Bureau with payment of renewal fees; renewals may be made electronically via the E‑renewal interface. Renewals may cover all or some designs and all or some designated Contracting Parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use E‑renewal for convenience and to selectively renew designs/territories. Ensure timely payment of renewal fees to avoid lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordable changes in the International Register
rubrics_metrics.description: The following changes may be recorded: (a) change in name and address of the holder; (b) change in ownership (in respect of all or some designated Parties and/or all or some designs); (c) renunciation of all designs in respect of any or all designated Parties; (d) limitation of some only of the designs in respect of any or all designated Parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests to record changes must be submitted on the relevant official form with prescribed fees. Recorded information is published in the Register/Bulletin for third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative advantages of the Hague system
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague system simplifies and economizes protection by replacing multiple national filings with a single international application: one language, one Office (WIPO), one set of fees and simpler subsequent management (e.g., recording changes centrally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Hague system to avoid managing multiple deadlines, fees in various currencies and differing procedures; weigh administrative efficiencies against the possibility of national substantive refusals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of additional information and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO's website provides the full Acts, Common Regulations, Guide to the International Registration of Designs, list of Contracting Parties, electronic filing/renewal interfaces, forms, current fees (including individual designation fees), fee calculator, International Designs Bulletin, Hague Express database, Locarno Classification, and annual statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult WIPO resources (forms, Guide, fee calculator, databases) for up‑to‑date procedural details and to prepare compliant filings.
